title: Why the World’s Climate Talks Broke Down—and What Happens Now
author: T Michelle Murphy
body:
COP31, the United Nations’ annual climate change summit, ended on Sunday without consensus on an overarching climate deal after about two days of overtime in Antalya, Türkiye.

The annual conference brings together delegates to shape and formalize an approach to combating the effects of global warming. This year, the main dispute was whether the agreement should explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels.

That commitment traces back to the Paris Agreement, a 2015 climate treaty that calls for efforts to limit global warming to 1.5°C (2.7°F) above preindustrial levels.

Among the countries that opposed language calling for a transition away from fossil fuels were Russia and Saudi Arabia, while the European Union, the United Kingdom, and others refused to agree to any deals that did not acknowledge the leading cause of climate change.

COP31’s President Murat Kurum announced on Sunday that a deal had not been reached.

“It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted,” he said.

Australia’s Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen was a co-leader at the event, acting as President of Negotiations. “Unfortunately we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision and that’s very disappointing,” he said Sunday.

Failure to reach an agreement is not unheard of, but it is uncommon; the last comparable deadlock was in Copenhagen in 2009. At the time, an irreconcilable clash emerged over which countries should cut greenhouse gas emissions, how deep those cuts should be, and whether the commitments should be legally binding.

“Despite the range of expectations among states going into COP31, no delegation left believing it had been a win,” says Lavanya Rajamani, a professor of international environmental law at the University of Oxford who helped draft the Paris Agreement.

For Rajamani, the impasse shows how far apart the science and the politics of climate action have become.

“While such divergences are not new to the process, the gap has never been wider,” she says.

The world is on track to imminently exceed 1.5°C of warming, Rajamani adds, just as governments are showing a “rapidly dwindling appetite” for difficult and potentially costly action. That puts growing strain on a summit built around consensus.

What is COP31?

The Conference of the Parties (COP) is the annual meeting of countries that are party to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.

The U.N. climate summit originated in Berlin in 1995. The host location typically rotates, with recent summits taking place in Dubai, United Arab Emirates (2023); Baku, Azerbaijan (2024); and Belém, Brazil (2025). COP31 was scheduled for Nov. 9 through Nov. 20 in Antalya, but overtime extended the summit some 50 hours through Sunday. It was the longest overrun in the history of the U.N. climate talks.

Most countries sent delegations to COP31. Israel’s environment ministry said its officials would participate remotely, citing security concerns about sending a delegation to Antalya. The United States did not send an official delegation for the second year in a row. In January 2026, it withdrew from the Paris Agreement.

As COP31 was preparing to open in early November, a White House official told Spectrum News that the summit “rejects reality” and said the Trump Administration was pursuing an “energy dominance agenda.”

In Antalya, the countries at the table faced a different question: how to turn years of climate pledges into action.

“Over the past few years, international climate negotiations have shifted from a focus on establishing rules and making promises to ensuring implementation and delivery. This phase was always going to be challenging—it is where the rubber hits the road,” Rajamani says.

Broad language can smooth over disagreements, she continues, but it gets harder to find common ground when countries have to decide what to do and who will pay for it.

Why did the COP31 climate talks break down?

One of the biggest disputes at COP31 was whether the agreement should explicitly call for a shift away from fossil fuels.

A draft released early Sunday would have been the first U.N. climate summit agreement to acknowledge that global warming is on track to exceed 1.5°C above preindustrial levels in the coming years. It also welcomed faster development of technologies that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, with the aim of eventually bringing warming back below that threshold.

The draft referred back to the 2023 Dubai agreement as a whole, without explicitly restating its call to transition away from fossil fuels.

“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said on behalf of the EU on Sunday.

Burning coal, oil, and gas is the main cause of global warming, according to the United Nations, accounting for around 68% of global greenhouse gas emissions and nearly 90% of all carbon dioxide emissions. That warming is making heat waves more intense and causing sea levels to rise.

“The question is not so much what an explicit mention would have accomplished, but what its absence would have implied,” Rajamani explains. “The 2023 UAE consensus recognized the need to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems—yet subsequent COP decisions have failed to advance, or even reaffirm, this commitment.”

Meanwhile, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said in its 2025 advisory opinion on climate change that failure to take appropriate action on fossil fuel production, consumption, exploration licences, and subsidies may constitute an internationally wrongful act, she points out.

“The 2026 Santa Marta Initiative on transitioning away from fossil fuels is also gaining momentum,” she adds, referring to an April 2026 conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, where 57 countries gathered to discuss how to move away from fossil fuels.

“Against this backdrop, omitting fossil fuels from a COP cover decision would signal a retreat from the transition,” Rajamani says. “Explicit language, provided it did not weaken the UAE Consensus, would instead have reinforced growing momentum and sent an important signal to markets and policymakers.”

Climate finance was another sticking point. The Least Developed Countries group said the draft fell short on funding to help vulnerable countries adapt to climate change. The African Group of Negotiators, which represents 54 African countries, questioned whether the proposed roadmap would deliver that funding. The group was still willing to accept the draft as a compromise.

Delegates rejected a separate draft decision on the Mitigation Work Programme, which gives countries a forum to discuss how to cut greenhouse gas emissions faster and where investment is needed. At COP31, countries disagreed over how long to extend the program and how closely to tie it to the U.N.’s global assessment of climate progress. Delegates ultimately rejected the draft decision.

Delegates did, however, reach agreement on a “just transition” decision, which focuses on how to make the move to a low-carbon economy fair to workers and communities affected by the shift. The dispute at COP31 was over what a U.N. mechanism to support that work should do, how it should operate, and how it would be funded. The decision leaves operational details to be worked out in 2027.

They also adopted separate decisions on the Adaptation Fund and the Global Goal on Adaptation.

Rajamani says the overarching deal fell apart in part because some countries were more willing than in the past to reject an agreement they saw as too weak. They worry that downplaying climate damage, while prioritizing technological fixes over urgent emissions cuts and support, could undermine climate action in the long run.

What happens next?

Rajamani observes a “growing frustration with the time-intensive, consensus-based negotiating process,” and she says that it yields weak outcomes that are “radically out of step with the science and the scale and severity of climate impacts already unfolding.”

Youth advocates voiced their own frustration at the summit’s closing session. Oumnia Anfer, a youth representative at COP31, took the floor to address negotiators. “You have let us down,” she said. “We refuse to bear the consequences of your lack of ambition.”

“Some states, including those most vulnerable to climate change, appear to have reached the limits of their patience with the process,” Rajamani explains. She points out that a failure to reach an agreement simply punts decisions further down the road, saying: “All these issues will return to the agenda at the next COP.”

COP32 is scheduled to take place in November 2027 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

“Parties will return for the next round of the boxing match in Addis Ababa next year,” Rajamani says. “In the meantime, growing frustration and exasperation with the multilateral negotiating process are likely to drive greater attention towards climate litigation—which has yielded far more progressive and climate-friendly outcomes, including at the highest judicial level, the ICJ—and climate action beyond the state.”

Ireland and Tuvalu plan to co-host a follow-up to the Santa Marta conference on moving away from fossil fuels before COP32.

Both meetings are months away. At Sunday’s closing session in Antalya, Kurum pointed to the urgency of the work still ahead.

“Climate change does not follow our negotiating schedule,” he said, before gaveling the summit to an end.
